::: {.callout-note .objectives}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- apply a function over the rows or columns of a matrix with `apply()`;
- iterate over lists and data frame columns with `lapply()`, `sapply()`, `vapply()` and their `purrr` equivalents;
- explain **type stability** and choose functions whose output type you can predict;
- apply a function **by group** with `tapply()` or `split()` + `map()`;
- fit one model per group and collect the results in a single table.
:::




::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(purrr)
library(tibble)
```
:::


## 1. Why iteration functions?

In [Loops](16-loops.qmd) you computed the mean of four penguin columns with a `for` loop. It needed five lines: create a container, name it, loop over positions, extract a column, store the result. Only one of those lines said what we actually wanted: *"the mean"*.

An **iteration function** (also called a *functional*) takes a function and applies it to every element of a vector or list, handling all the bookkeeping for you:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
num_cols <- penguins[, c("bill_len", "bill_dep", "flipper_len", "body_mass")]

sapply(num_cols, mean, na.rm = TRUE)                  # base R
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>    bill_len    bill_dep flipper_len   body_mass 
#>       43.92       17.15      200.92     4201.75
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
map_dbl(num_cols, \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE))         # purrr
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>    bill_len    bill_dep flipper_len   body_mass 
#>       43.92       17.15      200.92     4201.75
```


:::
:::


Both lines say "for each column, compute the mean". They are shorter, harder to get wrong, and easy to read. Under the hood they are still loops, so they are not magically faster; the gain is **clarity**.

## 2. `apply()`: rows and columns of a matrix

`apply(X, MARGIN, FUN, ...)` applies `FUN` to each row (`MARGIN = 1`) or each column (`MARGIN = 2`) of a matrix `X`. Extra arguments in `...` are passed on to `FUN`.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
m1 <- matrix(1:30, nrow = 5, ncol = 6)
m1
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5] [,6]
#> [1,]    1    6   11   16   21   26
#> [2,]    2    7   12   17   22   27
#> [3,]    3    8   13   18   23   28
#> [4,]    4    9   14   19   24   29
#> [5,]    5   10   15   20   25   30
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
apply(m1, 2, sum)       # one value per column
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1]  15  40  65  90 115 140
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
apply(m1, 1, max)       # one value per row
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 26 27 28 29 30
```


:::
:::


For sums and means there are dedicated (and faster) functions: `rowSums()`, `colSums()`, `rowMeans()`, `colMeans()`.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
colSums(m1)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1]  15  40  65  90 115 140
```


:::
:::


If `FUN` returns more than one value, `apply()` puts the results in the **columns** of a matrix, which is often transposed compared to what you expect:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
apply(m1, 2, range)     # 2 rows (min, max), one column per column of m1
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5] [,6]
#> [1,]    1    6   11   16   21   26
#> [2,]    5   10   15   20   25   30
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-warning}
## `apply()` on a data frame
`apply()` first converts a data frame into a **matrix**. If there is a single text or factor column, *everything* becomes text, and `mean()` returns `NA` with a warning. Use `apply()` for matrices; for data frames, use `lapply()`, `sapply()`, `map()` or `across()`.
:::

## 3. `lapply()`: always returns a list

`lapply(X, FUN, ...)` applies `FUN` to each element of `X` (a vector, a list or the columns of a data frame) and **always returns a list** of the same length.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
# cars ships with R; data() just makes the source explicit
data(cars, package = "datasets")
lapply(cars, range)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> $speed
#> [1]  4 25
#> 
#> $dist
#> [1]   2 120
```


:::
:::


Another example, with a character vector:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
movies <- c("SPYDERMAN", "BATMAN", "VERTIGO", "CHINATOWN")
movies_lower <- lapply(movies, tolower)
str(movies_lower)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> List of 4
#>  $ : chr "spyderman"
#>  $ : chr "batman"
#>  $ : chr "vertigo"
#>  $ : chr "chinatown"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
unlist(movies_lower)     # back to a character vector
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "spyderman" "batman"    "vertigo"   "chinatown"
```


:::
:::


(`tolower()` is already vectorised, so `tolower(movies)` gives the same character vector directly: iterate only when you need to.)

A list is the most flexible container: each element can have a different length or type. That flexibility is also the downside: you often want a plain vector instead.

## 4. `sapply()` and `vapply()`: simplify the result

`sapply()` calls `lapply()` and then tries to **simplify** the result into a vector or a matrix:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
sapply(cars, min)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> speed  dist 
#>     4     2
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
sapply(cars, range)      # each result has length 2 -> a 2-column matrix
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>      speed dist
#> [1,]     4    2
#> [2,]    25  120
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
avg_range <- function(x) (min(x) + max(x)) / 2
sapply(cars, avg_range)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> speed  dist 
#>  14.5  61.0
```


:::
:::


### The problem: type instability

What `sapply()` returns depends on **what the function returns**. If the results have different lengths, it silently gives a list instead:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
above_mean <- function(x) x[x > mean(x)]

res <- sapply(cars, above_mean)
class(res)               # a list, not a vector or matrix
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "list"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
lengths(res)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> speed  dist 
#>    24    21
```


:::
:::


And with an empty input it returns an empty *list*:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
sapply(list(), length)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> list()
```


:::
:::


A function whose output type depends on the input values is called **type unstable**. Interactively this is harmless; inside a function or a script it can cause errors far away from their cause.

### `vapply()`: say what you expect

`vapply()` adds an argument `FUN.VALUE` that describes the result of **each** call: `numeric(1)` (one number), `character(1)`, `logical(1)`, or `numeric(2)` for two numbers. If a result does not match, `vapply()` stops with an error immediately.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
vapply(cars, min, numeric(1))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> speed  dist 
#>     4     2
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
vapply(cars, range, numeric(2))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>      speed dist
#> [1,]     4    2
#> [2,]    25  120
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
vapply(cars, above_mean, numeric(1))     # error: lengths differ
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error}

```
#> Error in `vapply()`:
#> ! values must be length 1,
#>  but FUN(X[[1]]) result is length 24
```


:::
:::


Rule of thumb: `sapply()` at the console, `vapply()` (or `map_dbl()` & co., below) inside functions.

## 5. Applying a function by group: `tapply()`

`tapply(X, INDEX, FUN)` splits the vector `X` into groups defined by the factor `INDEX` and applies `FUN` to each group:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
tapply(iris$Sepal.Width, iris$Species, median)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>     setosa versicolor  virginica 
#>        3.4        2.8        3.0
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
tapply(penguins$body_mass, penguins$species, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>    Adelie Chinstrap    Gentoo 
#>      3701      3733      5076
```


:::
:::


With a **list** of two factors you get a two-way table:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
tapply(penguins$body_mass, list(penguins$species, penguins$sex), mean,
       na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>           female male
#> Adelie      3369 4043
#> Chinstrap   3527 3939
#> Gentoo      4680 5485
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output
Rows are species, columns are sexes, and each cell is the mean body mass of that combination. Males are heavier than females in every species. For data frames, `dplyr::summarise(.by = c(species, sex))` produces the same numbers in a tidy table: see [Grouped summaries](../02-data/10-grouped-summaries.qmd).
:::

## 6. Two inputs at once: `mapply()` and `Map()`

`lapply()` iterates over **one** vector. To iterate over two vectors in parallel (first with first, second with second…), use `mapply()` (simplifies like `sapply()`) or `Map()` (returns a list like `lapply()`):


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
means <- c(0, 10, 100)
sds   <- c(1, 2, 10)
set.seed(1)
Map(\(m, s) round(rnorm(3, mean = m, sd = s), 1), means, sds)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [[1]]
#> [1] -0.6  0.2 -0.8
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] 13.2 10.7  8.4
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> [1] 104.9 107.4 105.8
```


:::
:::


## 7. The modern way: `purrr`

The `purrr` package (part of the tidyverse) offers the same ideas with a **consistent and type-stable** interface. The function name tells you exactly what you get back:

| Base R | purrr | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `lapply(x, f)` | `map(x, f)` | a list |
| `vapply(x, f, numeric(1))` | `map_dbl(x, f)` | a numeric (double) vector |
| `vapply(x, f, character(1))` | `map_chr(x, f)` | a character vector |
| `vapply(x, f, logical(1))` | `map_lgl(x, f)` | a logical vector |
| `vapply(x, f, integer(1))` | `map_int(x, f)` | an integer vector |
| `Map(f, x, y)` / `mapply()` | `map2(x, y, f)` | a list (also `map2_dbl()`, …) |
| — | `imap(x, f)` | like `map()`, but `f` also receives the name |


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
map_dbl(cars, median)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> speed  dist 
#>    15    36
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
map_chr(penguins, \(col) class(col)[1])
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>     species      island    bill_len    bill_dep flipper_len   body_mass 
#>    "factor"    "factor"   "numeric"   "numeric"   "integer"   "integer" 
#>         sex        year 
#>    "factor"   "integer"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
map_lgl(penguins, anyNA)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>     species      island    bill_len    bill_dep flipper_len   body_mass 
#>       FALSE       FALSE        TRUE        TRUE        TRUE        TRUE 
#>         sex        year 
#>        TRUE       FALSE
```


:::
:::


`map_dbl()` *guarantees* a numeric vector of the same length as the input, or an error. There is no "sometimes a list" surprise.

Extra arguments: write an **anonymous function** `\(x) ...` rather than passing them after the function. It makes clear which argument is which:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
map_dbl(num_cols, \(x) sd(x, na.rm = TRUE))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>    bill_len    bill_dep flipper_len   body_mass 
#>       5.460       1.975      14.062     801.955
```


:::
:::


### `map2()` and `imap()`

`map2()` iterates over two inputs in parallel; `imap()` gives the function both the element and its **name** (or position):


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
map2_dbl(c(2, 3, 4), c(3, 2, 1), \(base, exp) base^exp)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 8 9 4
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
imap_chr(num_cols, \(x, name) paste0(name, ": ", sum(is.na(x)), " missing"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>                 bill_len                 bill_dep              flipper_len 
#>    "bill_len: 2 missing"    "bill_dep: 2 missing" "flipper_len: 2 missing" 
#>                body_mass 
#>   "body_mass: 2 missing"
```


:::
:::


### Combining data frames: `list_rbind()`

A very common pattern: compute a small data frame for each element, then stack them into one. `map()` gives a list of data frames and `list_rbind()` binds them by row:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
num_cols |>
  imap(\(x, name) tibble(
    variable = name,
    mean     = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd       = sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  )) |>
  list_rbind()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   variable       mean      sd
#>   <chr>         <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 bill_len      43.92   5.460
#> 2 bill_dep      17.15   1.975
#> 3 flipper_len  200.9   14.06 
#> 4 body_mass   4202.   802.0
```


:::
:::


This replaces the slow "grow a data frame with `rbind()` inside a loop" pattern (see [Loops](16-loops.qmd#loops-or-vectorisation)).

## 8. Applying a function by group: `split()` + `map()`

`split(df, df$group)` cuts a data frame into a **named list** of smaller data frames, one per group. Then any iteration function can process each piece:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
by_species <- split(penguins, penguins$species)
names(by_species)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "Adelie"    "Chinstrap" "Gentoo"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
map_int(by_species, nrow)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>    Adelie Chinstrap    Gentoo 
#>       152        68       124
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
map_dbl(by_species, \(d) cor(d$bill_len, d$bill_dep, use = "complete.obs"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>    Adelie Chinstrap    Gentoo 
#>    0.3915    0.6535    0.6434
```


:::
:::


All three correlations between bill length and bill depth are positive *within* species. (Across all penguins pooled together the correlation is *negative*, -0.24, an example of Simpson's paradox that you will meet again in [Correlation](../06-visualization/27-correlation.qmd).)

## 9. Mini-project: many models

Does body mass increase with flipper length at the **same rate** in every species? We fit one simple [linear regression](../09-regression/38-simple-regression.qmd) per species and compare the slopes. The slope of `lm(body_mass ~ flipper_len)` is the average increase in body mass (g) per extra millimetre of flipper.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
fits <- by_species |>
  map(\(d) lm(body_mass ~ flipper_len, data = d))

slopes <- map_dbl(fits, \(m) coef(m)[["flipper_len"]])
slopes
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>    Adelie Chinstrap    Gentoo 
#>     32.83     34.57     54.62
```


:::
:::


Now collect several results per model in one table:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
model_table <- fits |>
  imap(\(m, sp) tibble(
    species   = sp,
    n         = nobs(m),
    intercept = coef(m)[[1]],
    slope     = coef(m)[[2]],
    r_squared = summary(m)$r.squared
  )) |>
  list_rbind()

model_table
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>   species       n intercept slope r_squared
#>   <chr>     <int>     <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 Adelie      151    -2536. 32.83    0.2192
#> 2 Chinstrap    68    -3037. 34.57    0.4116
#> 3 Gentoo      123    -6787. 54.62    0.4937
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output
Each row is one model. In Gentoo penguins, body mass increases by about 55 g per mm of flipper; in Adelie by about 33 g, and in Chinstrap by about 35 g. `n` is the number of birds actually used (`lm()` drops rows with missing values), and `r_squared` is the share of the variation in body mass explained by flipper length within that species. Whether the slopes differ *more than chance would explain* is a question for [multiple regression](../09-regression/39-multiple-regression.qmd) with an interaction term.
:::

The same three-step recipe — **split, map, combine** — works for any per-group analysis: a t-test per country, a plot per year, a summary per file.

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: other ways to do the same
- `dplyr`: `penguins |> group_by(species) |> group_map(\(d, key) ...)` or `nest_by()`; `reframe()` for summaries returning several rows per group.
- `broom::tidy(m)` and `broom::glance(m)` turn a model into a one-row (or one-row-per-coefficient) data frame, so that `map(fits, broom::tidy) |> list_rbind(names_to = "species")` builds a complete coefficient table.
- `purrr::safely()` and `possibly()` wrap a function so that one failing group does not stop the whole iteration.
- `furrr` / `mirai` run `map()`-style iterations in parallel on several cores.
:::

::: {.callout-warning .pitfall}
## Common pitfalls

1. **`sapply()` returning a list when you expected a vector.** Use `vapply()` or `map_dbl()`/`map_chr()` so that surprises become errors.
2. **`apply()` on a data frame with text columns** turns everything into text. Select numeric columns first, or use `map_dbl()`/`across()`.
3. **Iterating when a vectorised function exists.** `sapply(x, sqrt)` is just `sqrt(x)`; `lapply(movies, tolower)` is just `tolower(movies)`.
4. **Forgetting that `apply(m, 2, range)` puts results in columns** (2 × ncol), not rows.
5. **`split()` with missing group values.** Rows whose group is `NA` are dropped silently from the list.
6. **Passing extra arguments in the wrong place.** `map_dbl(x, mean, na.rm = TRUE)` still works, but `\(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)` is clearer and is the style recommended by purrr.
:::

## 10. Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q1. What type of object does `lapply()` return? And `map_chr()`?

`lapply()` always returns a **list**. `map_chr()` always returns a **character vector** of the same length as the input (or an error).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q2. What is the result of `apply(matrix(1:6, nrow = 2), 1, sum)`?

The matrix has rows `1 3 5` and `2 4 6`, so the row sums are `9` and `12`.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q3. You have a list of 50 data frames (one per country) and want one table with a row per country. Which two `purrr` functions?

`map()` (or `imap()`, to keep the country name) to compute a one-row data frame per country, then `list_rbind()` to stack them.
:::

## 11. Exercises

### Interactive (run in your browser)

::: {.exercise}
[★]{.stars} **Exercise 1 — `apply()` on a matrix.** The built-in matrix `VADeaths` contains death rates per 1000 in Virginia (1940) by age group (rows) and population group (columns). Compute the **maximum of each column** and the **mean of each row**.


::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_17_1'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_17_1
VADeaths
apply(VADeaths, ______, max)
apply(VADeaths, ______, mean)
```
:::


::: {.hint exercise="ex_17_1"}
`MARGIN = 2` means columns, `MARGIN = 1` means rows.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_17_1"}
```r
apply(VADeaths, 2, max)
apply(VADeaths, 1, mean)   # same as rowMeans(VADeaths)
```
Death rates increase steadily with age: the row means grow from the youngest to the oldest group.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 2 — `map_*()` on columns.** For every column of `airquality`, compute (a) the number of missing values with `map_int()`, and (b) the median, ignoring missing values, with `map_dbl()`.


::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_17_2'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_17_2
library(purrr)
map_int(airquality, \(x) sum(______))
map_dbl(airquality, \(x) median(x, ______))
```
:::


::: {.hint exercise="ex_17_2"}
`is.na(x)` gives `TRUE` for each missing value; `sum()` counts them. For the median use `na.rm = TRUE`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_17_2"}
```r
map_int(airquality, \(x) sum(is.na(x)))
map_dbl(airquality, \(x) median(x, na.rm = TRUE))
```
`Ozone` has 37 missing values and `Solar.R` has 7; the other columns are complete. You will meet these missing values again in [Missing data](../04-io/20-missing-data.qmd).
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 3 — debug type instability.** This function is supposed to return, for each column of a data frame, its first value as text. It works on `mtcars` but returns an empty *list* on a data frame with no columns. Rewrite it with `vapply()` (or `map_chr()`) so that it always returns a character vector.


::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_17_3'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_17_3
first_values <- function(df) {
  sapply(df, \(x) as.character(x[1]))
}
str(first_values(mtcars[1:3]))
str(first_values(mtcars[0]))        # a data frame with zero columns
```
:::


::: {.hint exercise="ex_17_3"}
`vapply(df, \(x) as.character(x[1]), character(1))` declares that each result is one string.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_17_3"}
```r
first_values <- function(df) {
  vapply(df, \(x) as.character(x[1]), character(1))
}
str(first_values(mtcars[1:3]))   # named chr vector
str(first_values(mtcars[0]))     # Named chr(0): still a character vector
```
With zero columns `sapply()` has nothing to simplify and returns `list()`. `vapply()` knows the expected type even when there is nothing to compute.
:::

[★★★]{.stars} **Exercise 4 — many models.** Using `mtcars`, fit `lm(mpg ~ wt)` separately for cars with 4, 6 and 8 cylinders, and extract the slope of `wt` for each group. In which group does an extra 1000 lbs of weight cost the most miles per gallon?


::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_17_4'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_17_4
library(purrr)
by_cyl <- split(mtcars, ______)
fits <- map(by_cyl, \(d) lm(______, data = d))
map_dbl(fits, \(m) coef(m)[["wt"]])
```
:::


::: {.hint exercise="ex_17_4"}
Split by `mtcars$cyl`; the model formula is `mpg ~ wt`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_17_4"}
```r
by_cyl <- split(mtcars, mtcars$cyl)
fits <- map(by_cyl, \(d) lm(mpg ~ wt, data = d))
map_dbl(fits, \(m) coef(m)[["wt"]])
```
All slopes are negative (heavier cars use more fuel). The steepest slope is for 4-cylinder cars, about −5.6 mpg per 1000 lbs. With only 7–14 cars per group these slopes are very uncertain: look at `confint(fits[["4"]])` before drawing conclusions.

### Practice on your own computer

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 5 — a summary table for every column.** Write a function `describe_col(x)` that returns a one-row tibble with `n_missing`, `mean`, `sd`, `min` and `max` of a numeric vector. Use `imap()` + `list_rbind()` to build a table with one row per numeric column of `penguins` and a column `variable` with the column name.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
library(purrr)
library(tibble)

describe_col <- function(x) {
  tibble(
    n_missing = sum(is.na(x)),
    mean = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd   = sd(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    min  = min(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    max  = max(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}

penguins |>
  keep(is.numeric) |>                       # keep only numeric columns
  imap(\(x, name) tibble(variable = name, describe_col(x))) |>
  list_rbind()
```
`keep()` from purrr keeps the elements (here, columns) for which the predicate is `TRUE`; `penguins[sapply(penguins, is.numeric)]` is the base-R equivalent. `year` is numeric too, so it appears in the table — decide whether that makes sense.
:::
:::

## Summary

| Task | Base R | purrr |
|---|---|---|
| Rows/columns of a matrix | `apply(m, 1 or 2, f)`, `rowSums()`, `colMeans()` | — |
| Each element → list | `lapply(x, f)` | `map(x, f)` |
| Each element → vector of known type | `vapply(x, f, numeric(1))` | `map_dbl()`, `map_chr()`, `map_lgl()`, `map_int()` |
| Simplify if possible | `sapply(x, f)` | — |
| By group | `tapply(x, g, f)`, `split()` + `lapply()` | `split()` + `map()` |
| Two inputs in parallel | `Map()`, `mapply()` | `map2()` |
| Element and its name | — | `imap()` |
| Stack data frames | `do.call(rbind, lst)` | `list_rbind()` |

- Iteration functions express **what** to do to each element; the bookkeeping is done for you.
- Prefer **type-stable** functions (`vapply()`, `map_dbl()`, …) in scripts and functions.
- **Split → map → combine** handles any per-group analysis, including fitting many models.
- If a vectorised function exists, you do not need to iterate at all.
